title: The sign of the cross, slowly
hook: Father on the forehead, Son on the heart, Holy Spirit across the shoulders
carry: one god, three persons, one gesture

segments.voice: Yesterday, the communion of saints, and the close of the stories. Your line was so great a cloud of witnesses. Which saint did you pick to walk with? Now Camp Three: the practices. Day ninety-seven.

Watch a baseball player step up to the plate, or a soccer player run onto the pitch. Some of them touch forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other, fast, almost a flick. Watch a grandmother pass a church on the bus: the same gesture, small and quick. Watch someone hear bad news. The same. It might be the most common prayer on earth that people make without saying anything. Camp Two was the stories. Camp Three is the practices, what Catholics actually do with their bodies, their days, their Sundays. And it starts where a Catholic's prayer almost always starts: the sign of the cross. Today we slow it down.
screen: `A FLICK AT THE PLATE.` → `A GRANDMOTHER ON THE BUS.` → `CAMP THREE: THE PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: Here's the gesture, slowly. The right hand touches the forehead: in the name of the Father. Then down to the chest, over the heart: and of the Son. Then across, left shoulder to right: and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Two things are happening at once. The hand draws a cross on the body. And the mouth says a name. That name comes straight from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends his friends out. In the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Notice it says in the name, singular, not in the names. One name, three persons. That's today's word: the Trinity. Christians believe in one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three persons, not three gods, not three masks. Catholics call it a mystery, not because it's a riddle to give up on, but because it's deeper than anyone reaches the bottom of. And the sign of the cross puts the whole thing in five seconds, on your own body. It's old. Around the year 200, a writer in North Africa named Tertullian said Christians traced the sign on their foreheads at every coming and going, getting dressed, lighting lamps, sitting down. Most Catholics were baptized with these same words, so every time they make the sign, they're remembering that. One more detail: Latin Catholics cross left shoulder to right. Byzantine Catholics, like the Eastern Orthodox, go right to left. Same prayer, same cross.
screen: `FOREHEAD, HEART, SHOULDERS.` · `IN THE NAME, NOT THE NAMES.` · `ONE GOD, THREE PERSONS.` · `A GESTURE SINCE ABOUT 200 AD.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one sign, taking five seconds. Settle, and breathe. If you're a Catholic, or you'd like to try it, make the sign of the cross as slowly as you can. Forehead: pause. Heart: pause. Shoulder, and shoulder. Feel where your hand lands. If you'd rather not make the gesture, just picture it, or rest a hand on your chest. Then sit in the quiet it leaves. The bell holds the time.
Trinity. One God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the name Catholics trace on themselves every time they pray. Today's word.
Your line: one God, three persons, one gesture. Today, the next time you see someone make that quick sign, at a game or on a bus, you'll know everything inside it. Day ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics begin and end most prayers, and the Mass itself, with the sign of the cross; many also make it when passing a church, before meals, before a game or a test, or on hearing hard news.

fork.reveal: one name, singular, and three persons. that's the Trinity in a single phrase, and the words of the sign of the cross.

original.note: Latin: threeness, the Trinity. Tertullian is the earliest known writer to use it this way.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quick gesture for luck.
what it means: a prayer on the body: the cross traced, and the one name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit spoken.
what a scholar hears: in the name, singular, in Matthew 28:19. and the Latin word trinitas first appears in Tertullian, the same writer who describes the sign.

sources.quoted: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.

notes: Douay-Rheims Matthew 28:19 fragment given from memory; confirm.
Tertullian, De Corona 3, on tracing the sign on the forehead at every going out and coming in, dressing, lighting lamps, reclining: paraphrased; date c. 204. Confirm.
Tertullian as the earliest known Latin writer to use 'trinitas' (Against Praxeas); Theophilus of Antioch used Greek 'trias' earlier. Confirm the game note.
Direction of the crossing (Latin left-to-right; Eastern right-to-left): confirm the description of Eastern Catholic practice.
The voice uses 'Holy Spirit' in the gesture and quotes 'Holy Ghost' from the Douay-Rheims; both are traditional.

Audit (2026-09-30): the teach and myth said all Eastern Catholics cross right to left like 'the Orthodox'; that is true of the Byzantine churches, but some Eastern churches (e.g. Armenian, Coptic) cross left to right. Narrowed to 'Byzantine Catholics, like the Eastern Orthodox'.
